# Sensory Support Planning Guide

Fictional Cedar Lantern Dance Studio. Training fixture only; no real studio policy.

## Requesting a learning adjustment
The sensory support plan records practical choices that help a student take part in a dance class. It is a collaboration with the student and, where appropriate, the guardian. A student can request a quieter explanation without supplying a diagnosis. Teachers discuss arrangements privately, use the student's preferred words and check whether the agreed support still helps after the first sessions.

A planned sensory adjustment request should reach the support coordinator five business days before the relevant class. A late request is still heard and the teacher considers what can be arranged safely that day; the lead time is not a reason to refuse to listen. The plan states the activity, support choice and review date. Personal background details are kept out of a public class notice.

An agreed sensory support plan is reviewed after the student's first three attended classes. Missed classes do not count towards this review point. The student can ask for an earlier conversation if the arrangement is uncomfortable or impractical. A review can retain, change or stop a support choice; it is not an automatic withdrawal of support. The coordinator records the decision and the student's own feedback where possible.

## Hearing protection and the emergency signal
A student may wear their own ear defenders during ordinary class exercises after the teacher confirms a visible stop signal. The teacher rehearses the signal with the student before a sequence begins. The room-operation notes set a narrow condition during an evacuation drill; the ordinary class permission must be considered together with that condition. Headphones playing private music are not automatically covered by permission for passive ear defenders.

Teachers should give a spoken and visible cue for a planned loud activity. A student can choose an alternative position agreed in the plan. Do not make another child responsible for continuously interpreting the stop signal. If the visibility arrangement fails, pause the activity and agree a workable signal rather than removing the student's support without explanation.

## Quiet room duration conflict
The sensory planning guide permits a quiet-room break of up to 15 minutes before a teacher check-in. The current quiet-room operation notes give a different interval for the same ordinary break. Neither current document establishes a precedence rule. Show both intervals to the coordinator and avoid inventing separate age groups or treating one as an emergency-only rule. A 15 minute intermission in a show programme is unrelated to this support check-in.

## Communication and leaving an activity
A student can show the blue pause card to request a supported break without first explaining the reason aloud. The teacher acknowledges the card and follows the agreed movement route. The card is not a permission to leave the building alone. Where the room lead needs to account for a student, the teacher records the move in the private class register rather than displaying a public list of support users.

An accompanying adult follows the recorded plan and the room's supervision rules. A friend can walk beside the student if staff agree, but friendship does not replace adult supervision. When the student returns, offer a short factual update about the exercise rather than asking them to justify the break in front of peers. A support tool should not become a reward to earn or a penalty to lose.

## Planning an unfamiliar class
For a guest class, the coordinator shares only the practical support steps the visiting teacher needs. The guest does not receive the student's whole personal history. The teacher checks the visible signal in the unfamiliar room and points out the route to the quiet seat. If the usual room is unavailable, the coordinator agrees another supervised place before promising the same arrangement. A change of teacher is a reason to brief the plan clearly, not to assume every adjustment starts again from nothing.

## A participation example
Lea uses passive ear defenders, a visible stop signal and a blue pause card. Her teacher rehearses the signal, offers a position with a clear view, and acknowledges a card without demanding an announcement. After her third attended class, Lea and the coordinator review whether the cue is easy to see. An evacuation drill uses the room-operation condition as well as the ordinary ear-defender permission. Before confirming a break interval to her guardian, the coordinator must reconcile the two current quiet-room instructions rather than guessing which number was intended.

## Choice and privacy
A support plan can be read aloud privately if that helps the student participate in making it. Ask which practical words are useful rather than requiring a formal diagnostic vocabulary. A student may change their mind about a tactile object while keeping a visible cue. That does not mean the whole plan has failed. Staff can note a preference and revisit it at review. Copies shared with a substitute teacher should contain the support steps needed for that class and omit background details that do not help the teacher carry out those steps.

## New sounds and unfamiliar spaces
Before moving a class to a larger hall, the teacher explains any echo, different lighting or unfamiliar doorway. A student can look at the space with a supporting adult before the main group enters. The coordinator checks whether the usual pause route is still clear. A photo of a room can help explain a layout, but staff should not photograph another student's support visit as an example. The guide does not guarantee identical sensory conditions in every venue, and a useful adjustment should be checked in the actual room.
